title: The stories we tell, Assessment
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that school leaders should use storytelling to build shared understanding of assessment among staff, citing Willingham on stories being easier to understand and remember and Coyle on filling the windscreen with stories. He notes that assessment practices often persist unchallenged because they serve data-reporting purposes rather than teaching, and that data entry is a workload burden teachers report. He then organises the assessment story around three features of good stories: conflict (big questions such as what progress is and why we assess), causality (every assessment needs a stated reason, with the rationale revealed to teachers) and complications (reliability and validity, illustrated by invalid inferences such as confident hands-up answers meaning everyone understands). Leaders need real assessment knowledge to tell these stories well. The piece closes with two practices: run a thought experiment about what would happen if current data practices vanished, and rehearse the stories repeatedly so colleague feedback improves them.
points: Stories are an effective leadership tool for aligning staff beliefs about assessment because they are easier to understand and remember.
Assessment practices tend to persist unchallenged when they serve scrutiny and data reporting rather than teaching, so leaders must justify each one.
The conflict, causality and complications frame turns abstract assessment issues into a narrative staff can engage with and challenge.
Leaders need grounding in formative assessment, reliability and validity to tell these stories credibly, and the invalid-inference examples work as cautionary tales.
Rehearsing the stories often, and asking what would happen if the data vanished, surfaces unnecessary practices and strengthens the message.
quotes: Daniel Willingham tells us that stories are psychologically privileged and two of the reasons that it is useful for leaders to tell stories is that they are easier to understand and they are easier to remember. Daniel Coyle tells us that to establish purpose, we should ‘fill the windscreen with stories’ because this can help to build mental models which drive others’ behaviour.

Leaders have decisions to make about what teachers should assess and why. It is so easy to have assessment practices that persist for years unchallenged because they serve purposes other the bread and butter of teaching, the most significant example of which is when we ask teachers to make assessments so that we can present data for scrutiny as part of judgements of school effectiveness.

Setting up conflict with big questions such as these gets people talking and thinking. It brings to life a crucial aspect of school life and forces us as leaders into carefully reasoned justifications of all the decisions that we make.

Our assessment are not in spreadsheets for Ofsted or governors. Our assessments are to tailor our teaching. Our assessments are to intervene at the right moment to address misconceptions or to provide a timely word of encouragement.

We complete standardised tests twice a year to benchmark against other children nationally. Because standardised tests do not and can never directly assess our curriculum, teachers do not spend valuable time marking tests and analysing or inputting data.

Another useful thing to do is to practise telling the stories! Story tellers get better with each iteration and so if colleagues need to understand assessment practices and school leaders want to influence behaviour, these stories need to be told often.
